topStories.headline: After a Decade of Delays, Demolition Begins This Week at the Divisadero Car Wash
topStories.dek: Public Works permits list October 19 as the construction-start date for Greystar's 203-apartment building at the long-vacant 400 Divisadero site.
topStories.body:
The corner of Divisadero and Oak streets — a source of neighborhood frustration for nearly a decade — is finally coming down this week. Public Works has issued permits for construction-related sidewalk and street closures along the Divisadero and Oak frontages, with October 19 listed as the start date, and a demolition permit for the former Touchless Car Wash is also in process, according to the San Francisco Chronicle and SFist.

Greystar, the largest apartment developer in the United States, is under contract to acquire the site from original developer 4Terra Investments and has secured financing for the project. The planned eight-story building will hold 203 apartments — including 20 deed-restricted affordable units — roughly 1,850 square feet of ground-floor retail, parking for 24 cars, and storage for 144 bicycles.

The project was first approved in 2017 but sat stalled for nine years through multiple developer changes, political battles over whether to build market-rate or 100 percent affordable housing, and permit hurdles. District 5 Supervisor Bilal Mahmood worked with 4Terra to remove a key bureaucratic obstacle, and a 2026 state law allowing more flexible permit extensions helped clear the final path to construction.

Pedestrians and riders near Divisadero and Oak should expect ongoing sidewalk and partial lane closures as demolition and foundation work proceed. When complete, the project will be the largest housing development along the Divisadero corridor and in the Lower Haight.

topStories.headline: SF Planning Survey Opens as HVNA States Its 'Long-Term Vision' for Hayes Street
topStories.dek: The permit holder for the Hayes Street weekend closure has publicly described a goal of permanent pedestrianization, while a city-funded Public Life Study is already underway — and a neighborhood transportation meeting is set for October 22.
topStories.body:
The debate over the future of the 400 block of Hayes Street is moving into a more formal phase. The Hayes Valley Merchants Council's September newsletter encouraged businesses to participate in SF Planning's Public Life Study survey on the closure. In the same newsletter, the HVNA — the permit holder for the weekend closure, branded as Hayes Promenade — described its goal as creating "a pedestrian-forward model of Hayes Street that works for pedestrians, businesses, and some motor vehicles when necessary," according to Hayes Valley Safe, a neighborhood advocacy organization that published the detail on October 3.

Public records show that District 5 Supervisor Bilal Mahmood directly requested and drove the city's initiation of the Public Life Study, with the Planning Department leading technical work in coordination with SFMTA, SFCTA, and the Supervisor's office. Critics, including Hayes Valley Safe, argue that the $410,000 study — funded by restricted Prop I freeway-removal dollars — is scoped around an assumption that the shared space remains closed, and that residents and merchants have not been meaningfully included in the decision-making process.

The closure itself remains officially temporary: Hayes Street between Gough and Octavia is closed to traffic every Friday from 4 to 10 p.m. and every Saturday from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. through the remainder of 2026, per SFMTA. The outbound 6 Hayes/Parnassus Muni route is rerouted via Grove Street during closure hours.

Residents who want to engage directly can attend HVNA's community transportation and safety update on Thursday, October 22, at 6:30 p.m. Check hayesvalleysf.org for the venue.

topStories.headline: Theatre Flamenco Celebrates 60 Years with a One-Night Anniversary Show at Herbst
topStories.dek: San Francisco's oldest continuously operating flamenco company premieres 'De Ayer a Hoy' on Saturday, October 17, with nine works, three world premieres, and a post-show gala.
topStories.body:
Theatre Flamenco of San Francisco — founded by Adela Clara in 1966 and recognized by the San Francisco Chronicle as the oldest continuously operating flamenco company in the United States — marks its 60th anniversary this Saturday with a single performance at Herbst Theatre. The program, titled De Ayer a Hoy / From Yesterday to Today, consists of nine pieces: three world premieres and six reimaginings drawn from the company's six-decade repertoire.

Artistic director Carola Zertuche, who has led the company for 20 years, is joined by an international cast including flamenco dancer and choreographer Adrián Santana from Spain, San Francisco-based Cristina Hall performing a newly commissioned work, contemporary dancer Nol Simonse, singers Amparo Heredia and José "Cachito" Díaz, guitarist Jesse Torre, percussionist Diego Álvarez, and electronic musician Pascual Martínez.

The anniversary carries an elegiac dimension: founder Adela Clara died in May 2026 at 93, and former artistic director Miguel Santos, who handed the reins to Zertuche, died in 2024 at age 99. A post-performance gala in the Green Room of the War Memorial and Performing Arts Center follows the show at 9:30 p.m.

General admission tickets start at $45; VIP tickets, which include gala access, are $300. Tickets and information are available at theatreflamenco.org. The HVNA calendar lists the show as a Hayes Valley neighborhood event.

moreNews.headline: Huckberry Opens First San Francisco Store at 425 Hayes Street
moreNews.body: Huckberry, the outdoor-and-menswear brand founded in San Francisco roughly 15 years ago, opened its first brick-and-mortar store in the city at 425 Hayes Street in Hayes Valley on October 5, 2026, according to the company's own journal. The shop occupies the former Allbirds flagship space and operates Monday through Saturday 10 a.m.–7 p.m. and Sunday 10 a.m.–6 p.m. Hoodline first reported the lease signing in May; CoStar described the Hayes Valley debut, published October 8, as Huckberry's third U.S. store and part of a broader retail expansion.
